A.explanation: The $2\text{ V}$ drop from Q to S and $4\text{ V}$ drop from S to R satisfy both loop sums from P to R.

B.explanation: The Q to S value of $2\text{ V}$ is correct but $10\text{ V}$ for S to R would make the lower P to R route $15\text{ V}$, not equal to the upper $9\text{ V}$ route.

C.explanation: $3\text{ V}$ for Q to S ignores that P to Q is $3\text{ V}$ while P to S is $5\text{ V}$, so Q must be $2\text{ V}$ above S.

D.explanation: Both values are wrong because they do not conserve energy around the P-Q-S loop or along the two P to R paths.

hints: Notice the current is from P to R, so potential must fall going from P toward R along both the upper P-Q-R path and the lower P-S-R path.
Compare the two given drops from P: $3\text{ V}$ to Q and $5\text{ V}$ to S, to decide which of Q or S is at higher potential and by how much.
Add the upper-route drops P to Q and Q to R to get total P to R, then require the lower route P to S plus S to R to give the same total.
walkthrough: Take potential to fall in the direction of current. Let $V_P$ be the highest potential. Then $V_Q = V_P - 3\text{ V}$ and $V_S = V_P - 5\text{ V}$.
Subtract to find Q relative to S: $V_Q - V_S = (V_P - 3\text{ V}) - (V_P - 5\text{ V}) = 2\text{ V}$. So the p.d. between Q and S is $2\text{ V}$ with Q higher.
Find the total drop from P to R along the top path: $V_P - V_R = (V_P - V_Q) + (V_Q - V_R) = 3\text{ V} + 6\text{ V} = 9\text{ V}$.
The bottom path P to S to R must give the same total drop by Kirchhoff's voltage law: $(V_P - V_S) + (V_S - V_R) = 9\text{ V}$.
Substitute $V_P - V_S = 5\text{ V}$: $5\text{ V} + (V_S - V_R) = 9\text{ V}$, so $V_S - V_R = 4\text{ V}$. The p.d. between S and R is $4\text{ V}$.
A $2\text{ V}$ Q to S drop and a $4\text{ V}$ S to R drop matches the table. This is option A.
